TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving

Shuhuai Li Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University    Shengdong Ye Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University    Dongdong Ge Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University    Yinyu Ye Affiliation: Stanford University    Jianghao Lin ††thanks: Corresponding author. E-mail: linjianghao@sjtu.edu.cn. Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract

Agentic services alternate between model inference on clustered GPUs and external tools on distributed CPUs. In this scenario, existing systems (1) overlook tool-return readiness in service evaluation, wasting limited resources, and (2) use heuristic strategies to decide admission and placement on GPUs, resulting in suboptimal scheduling decisions. To bridge this gap, we present TAO, a tool-aware joint scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving. Its value interface combines near-term tool readiness, node-specific cache credit with time-aware decay, and token footprint; a dynamic program jointly selects and places waiting sessions under capacity constraints. Across the 12 reported model–workload–concurrency settings, TAO reduces latency by up to 26.8%, reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by up to 36.3%, and increases decode throughput by up to 29.5% relative to the best evaluated state-of-the-art baseline for each metric.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in language models have expanded their use beyond basic chatbots to complex agents, making CPU-based tool execution a substantial source of latency alongside GPU-based inference (Qiao et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). Specifically, an agent operates through an agent session that alternates between LLM inference and external tools, such as compilers and retrievers, to complete multi-step tasks (Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026). When tools run outside the inference service, a session’s demand for GPU computation becomes interruptible. We call this serving scenario Clustered-GPUs with Distributed-CPUs (CGDC), illustrated in Figure 1(Left): clustered GPUs, i.e., nodes, provide shared inference capacity, while external tool calls introduce delays between LLM requests11 1 One agent session consists of multiple LLM inference requests (i.e., steps) after tool calls.. Hence, efficient agentic serving must account for both inference demand and tool timing to sustain throughput and session responsiveness.

We find that existing serving systems generally follow an evaluate-then-decide scheduling pattern (Guy et al., 2025; SGLang Team, n.d.; vLLM Production Stack Team, n.d.). They evaluate node features at the session level and then decide where and when to serve each session. This separates the problem into two related challenges: (1) how to value a session’s next model turn, and (2) how to select and place sessions under shared capacity constraints.

For session evaluation, existing systems in CGDC scenarios generally overlook tool-call latency when evaluating established workload features. Cache-aware systems reuse KV prefixes and balance inference load (Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2025); workflow-aware systems anticipate future calls (Wadlom et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026); and latency-aware schedulers prioritize sessions using latency or remaining-work estimates (Choi et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Tool timing provides another useful signal, yet timing is utilized only as a surrogate for KV reuse or token count: Li et al. (2025) predicts tool duration to choose KV-cache retention times, while Kang et al. (2026) discounts the token footprint of sessions executing tools as time elapses. Such features commonly enter fixed scoring rules or manually chosen thresholds.

For decision making, existing systems usually apply heuristic scheduling strategies to each session, leading to myopic and suboptimal placements. In llm-d and SGLang (Guy et al., 2025; SGLang Team, n.d.), per-session scoring and routing rules assign inference opportunities individually. Yet sessions compete for the same node capacity. In particular, assigning one session can prevent a more valuable combination of other sessions from being served. Furthermore, the heuristic selection and placement rules can also lead to suboptimal choices (Peng et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). As shown in Figure 1(Right), they fail to formulate scheduling jointly across multiple sessions.

To address these challenges, we propose TAO, a Tool-Aware jOint scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving. To incorporate tool latency into session evaluation, we propose tool-return readiness and explicitly integrate it with established features such as KV-cache reuse. Following Kang et al. (2026), we interrupt sessions during tool calls and put them into a waiting pool. Tool-return readiness estimates which sessions will need inference within the next scheduling window. For each session–node pair, we form a value triplet from readiness, time-decayed KV-cache reuse, and token footprint. Given these evaluation triplets, we design a joint scheduling algorithm in the decision making stage that considers all sessions in the waiting pool. Across deployments in different scenarios, joint optimization considers how the admission of each session affects the placements available to others. The optimizer maximizes the additive evaluation triplets using dynamic programming. Their coordinates evolve with cache age and tool progress, allowing distinct signals to guide decisions over time without a weighted sum. Separating the optimization procedure from session evaluation makes the framework extensible.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

  • •

    We identify the Clustered GPUs with Distributed CPUs (CGDC) serving scenario in the era of LLM-based agents, which shifts the key bottleneck of latency to tool calls.

  • •

    We propose TAO, a tool-aware joint scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving. It improves the evaluate-then-decide paradigm through session evaluation with explicit tool-return readiness and decision making with joint modeling and optimization.

  • •

    TAO can be generalized and extended to different workloads such as multi-agent orchestration and Looped Agents. Moreover, it is also compatible with non-agent chatbot scenarios.

  • •

    Across the 12 reported model–workload–concurrency settings, TAO reduces latency by up to 26.8%, reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by up to 36.3%, and increases decode throughput by up to 29.5% relative to the state-of-the-art baseline for each metric.

2 Background and Problem Description

2.1 Agent Session and distributed resources

An agent session is a persistent interaction that alternates between model requests and external tool calls. During a model request, it uses a serving node; during tool execution, it awaits a result outside the inference service. A scheduler records each session’s state and controls session admission, while the serving engine manages physical KV-cache residency and eviction.

A later model request can reuse the KV prefix produced by earlier turns and avoid prefill computation (Kwon et al., 2023). Because an agent session carries its instructions, history, and tool observations across turns, reuse depends on both the agent session history and the node selected for its next request. SGLang and Preble exploit related prefix structure in model programs and distributed scheduling (Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025).

Our CGDC separates clustered GPU inference from distributed tool execution. Client or remote tools introduce variable delays between model requests, while their CPU and RAM are managed outside the GPU admission budget (Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026; Chang et al., 2026). Tool latency therefore determines when an agent session may need GPU resources for inference again.

2.2 session interruption and session restart

During tool execution, a session can release its GPU resources safely, although its cached prefix may subsequently be evicted. In contrast, preempting an active inference session requires recomputation. Repeated recomputation and reconstruction cause KV-cache thrashing, wasting capacity on state that must be rebuilt. This phenomenon motivates cache-aware engine and scheduling work (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2025), as well as policies that weigh retaining state against serving other work (Li et al., 2025; Abhyankar et al., 2024).

Therefore, at a tool boundary, the scheduler can apply session interruption. Specifically, a scheduler can interrupt the agent session’s model admission and release its node resources while the external tool continues. When inference service is needed again, session restarting restores admission on an eligible node and resumes the existing interaction. Session interruption and session restarting describe session state transitions. They are decoupled from the underlying inference engine.

We find that the decisions made for these two operations can be based on the same session evaluation. Thus, we optimize toward a unified goal for maximizing the evaluation. Session interruption can be decided by ordering sessions according to their values. Interrupted sessions join new arrivals in a waiting pool. We focus on unified session evaluation and restarting decisions from this pool.

3 Method

3.1 Framework overview

We present TAO, which combines agentic session evaluation with decision making, i.e. dynamic programming for joint selection and placement. The detailed formulation appears in Section 3.2.

Figure 2 illustrates the pipeline of our method. First, session evaluation maps agent session and node observations to assignment values (Section 3.2), including KV cache with time-aware decay (Section 3.3) and tool-return readiness (Section 3.4). Second, an exact dynamic program jointly selects waiting agent sessions and assigns them to nodes under residual capacity constraints (Sections 3.2 and 3.5). Separating session evaluation from decision making lets the evaluation interface evolve while preserving the scheduling procedure.

3.2 Formulation and Agentic session evaluation

At each restart scheduling decision, let the waiting pool PP contain the agent sessions awaiting inference admission, including interrupted sessions and new arrivals. Let BB be the nodes in the frozen snapshot. Each agent session ii has admission cost wiw_{i}, and each node bb has residual capacity CbC_{b}. Let E⊆P×BE\subseteq P\times B denote eligible assignments, and let xi,b∈{0,1}x_{i,b}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether session ii is admitted to node bb. The feasible set is

𝒳={x:∑b∈Bxi,b≤1,∑i∈Pwixi,b≤Cb,xi,b=0if (i,b)∉E}.\mathcal{X}=\left\{x:\sum_{b\in B}x_{i,b}\leq 1,\quad\sum_{i\in P}w_{i}x_{i,b}\leq C_{b},\quad x_{i,b}=0\ \text{if }(i,b)\notin E\right\}. (1)

TAO assigns each agent session–node pair the lexicographic value

𝒗i,b=(ki,b,ri,ti),\bm{v}_{i,b}=(k_{i,b},r_{i},t_{i}), (2)

where ki,bk_{i,b} is decayed cache credit, rir_{i} is the binary readiness signal, and tit_{i} is token count. We jointly select and place sessions to maximize their aggregate value:

x⋆∈arg​lexmaxx∈𝒳​∑i∈P∑b∈Bxi,b​𝒗i,b.x^{\star}\in\underset{x\in\mathcal{X}}{\operatorname{arg\,lexmax}}\sum_{i\in P}\sum_{b\in B}x_{i,b}\bm{v}_{i,b}. (3)

The evaluation triplet’s order remains fixed while its values evolve over time. Our design rationale is detailed as follows:

  • •

    KV-Cache credit takes precedence, but its value decays quickly after interruption, because prefix reuse directly avoids repeated prefill, motivating cache-aware scheduling (NVIDIA, 2025). The age-based discount in Section 3.3 favors recent cache evidence, which is often most useful when a tool returns quickly.

  • •

    As unrefreshed credit decays and the first component is equalized, tool-return readiness can distinguish agent sessions nearing a return from those still far from their next model turn (Section 3.4).

  • •

    Token footprint then favors larger accumulated contexts among plans tied on cache credit and readiness. The optimizer accounts for the greater capacity cost of such contexts when choosing the complete set of assignments.

3.3 Time-aware cache value for Clustered GPUs

TAO estimates reusable KV state from observations associated with each target node. It uses an observed cached-token count when available, or estimates the count from observed token volume and cache rate. A node without matching evidence receives zero credit. Figure 3 reports observed cache-token retention in DeepSeek-V4 Flash traces from two nodes with 4×4\timesH100 per node; the decline in binned medians motivates discounting older observations. Points show binned medians with bootstrap 95% intervals; the curve is a descriptive exponential fit over the populated bins through 1,800 s. Older observations receive less credit:

ki,b(t)=k0i,b 2−τi,b/h,\displaystyle k_{i,b}(t)=k^{0}_{i,b}\,2^{-\tau_{i,b}/h}, (4)
τi,b=max⁡(0,t−ti,bobs).\displaystyle\tau_{i,b}=\max(0,t-t^{\mathrm{obs}}_{i,b}).

Here ki,b0k^{0}_{i,b} is the observed cache credit and hh is its decay half-life. We use h=10h=10 seconds and round the resulting credit for valuation. The discount makes the admission value responsive to observation age; the serving engine continues to control physical allocation, reuse, and eviction. The half-life is a scheduler parameter, distinct from the fitted trace time constant. Dynamo similarly adjusts overlap value under excess prefill load, and ThunderAgent discounts token demand over time (NVIDIA, 2025; Kang et al., 2026).

3.4 Tool-return readiness in a distributed CPU

In our CGDC deployment, external executors manage tool CPU and RAM, while TAO controls GPU admission. Tool-return readiness connects these resource domains by identifying sessions likely to request model service within a short horizon. Tool timing reflects external execution conditions; the GPU admission budget accounts for the returning session’s inference footprint. Tool interfaces can expose progress or return deadlines: Claude Code’s Monitor forwards background-work events, while OpenCode reports termination after a Bash timeout (Anthropic, 2026a; OpenCode Contributors, 2026).

The predictor combines these hints, parsed sleep commands, and historical tool durations, using direct timing evidence first and falling back to the tool-specific history, global history, or a five-second default (Li et al., 2025). For a call with elapsed time ei​(t)e_{i}(t), the historical estimate D^f\widehat{D}_{f} gives

d^i​(t)=max⁡{0,D^f−ei​(t)}.\widehat{d}_{i}(t)=\max\{0,\widehat{D}_{f}-e_{i}(t)\}. (5)

The implementation adds a finite-sample margin to the historical mean; Appendix A specifies this estimator in detail.

Binary readiness. Let oi​(t)o_{i}(t) indicate observed tool completion, ai​(t)a_{i}(t) indicate an established tool execution candidate with an eligible prediction source, and gi​(t)g_{i}(t) indicate valid prediction timestamps refreshed within 30 seconds. Write zi​(t)z_{i}(t) for the earlier available predicted completion or exposed return deadline, treating an unavailable deadline as +∞+\infty. With horizon HH and overdue-probe indicator bi​(t)b_{i}(t), we define

ri​(t)={1,oi​(t)=1,ai​(t)​bi​(t),oi(t)=0,zi(t)≤t,ai(t)gi(t)𝟏[zi(t)≤t+H],otherwise.r_{i}(t)=\begin{cases}1,&o_{i}(t)=1,\\ a_{i}(t)b_{i}(t),&o_{i}(t)=0,\ z_{i}(t)\leq t,\\ a_{i}(t)g_{i}(t)\mathbf{1}[z_{i}(t)\leq t+H],&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (6)

TAO uses H=1H=1 second; the scheduler’s session interruption valuation uses its configured scheduling interval. Overdue predictions receive temporary probe opportunities instead of remaining ready indefinitely. Observed completion takes precedence over prediction checks. This signal prioritizes near-term returns among plans tied on higher-precedence values.

3.5 Joint scheduling with dynamic programming

The optimizer is a capacity-state dynamic program for the multiple-knapsack and generalized-assignment structure (Kellerer et al., 2004; Shmoys and Tardos, 1993). Let Δ\Delta be the capacity quantum, w¯i=⌈wi/Δ⌉\bar{w}_{i}=\lceil w_{i}/\Delta\rceil, and C¯b=⌊Cb/Δ⌋\bar{C}_{b}=\lfloor C_{b}/\Delta\rfloor. For candidate jj, let Dj​(𝒔)D_{j}(\bm{s}) be the best objective attainable from the first jj candidates at the used capacity 𝒔\bm{s}, and let 𝒖j,b\bm{u}_{j,b} embed the value and count for assigning jj to node bb:

Dj​(𝒔)=lexmax{Dj−1​(𝒔),maxb​eligiblelex​[Dj−1​(𝒔−w¯j​𝒆b)+𝒖j,b]}.D_{j}(\bm{s})=\mathop{\mathrm{lexmax}}\left\{D_{j-1}(\bm{s}),\;\max_{b\ \mathrm{eligible}}^{\mathrm{lex}}\left[D_{j-1}(\bm{s}-\bar{w}_{j}\bm{e}_{b})+\bm{u}_{j,b}\right]\right\}. (7)

Only nonnegative states within 𝑪¯\bar{\bm{C}} are allowed; D0​(𝟎)=𝟎D_{0}(\bm{0})=\bm{0} and other initial states are unreachable. Skipping or assigning each candidate exhausts the feasible choices, so induction gives exactness for the frozen, discretized problem; rounding can exclude plans feasible before discretization.

Node-specific cache observations are decayed and folded into assignment values during O⁡(n​m)O(nm) preprocessing; cache-equivalent nodes can be grouped into g≤mg\leq m aggregate capacity dimensions without moving physical KV blocks. The planner runs in an isolated asynchronous worker (detailed in Appendix B) and revalidates before application; recorded preparation plus completed-solve work is below 0.12% of runtime in the four-replica sweep (Appendix I).

4 Experiments

4.1 Experiment Setup

Models and workloads. We evaluate DeepSeek-V4 Flash, Qwen3-32B, and GLM-4.7 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025) on the SWE-bench Lite workload (SWE-Lite) using the mini-SWE-agent harness (MiniSWE) (mini-SWE-agent Contributors, 2026; Jimenez et al., 2024). For DeepSeek, we also use Claude Code on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026) for challenging tasks. For Qwen, we test with SWE-verified to exercise the serving capacity of its smaller model replicas. We further evaluate GLM-4.7 on SWE-Lite to test single-node performance. Appendix F reports an InferenceX trace-replay evaluation.

Deployment. DeepSeek runs on 2 nodes with 4×4\timesH100 per node; Qwen runs on 4 nodes with 2×2\timesH100 per node. Each node hosts one tensor-parallel model replica. GLM-4.7 runs on one node with 8×8\timesH100. Appendix E.1 reports a lower-concurrency DeepSeek check on the same single-node topology.

Baselines. vLLM Scheduler w/ RR and vLLM Scheduler w/ CA denote the vLLM schedulers with round-robin and cache-aware policies, respectively (vLLM Production Stack Team, n.d.), which align with the policy in SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024). These baselines cover load spreading and prefix-locality scheduling. Dynamo is a KV-aware scheduler (NVIDIA, 2025). ThunderAgent uses token-count scheduling and best-fit-decreasing placement (Kang et al., 2026). TAO combines predictive cache-aware session evaluation with joint dynamic-programming placement.

Metrics. We report mean task end-to-end latency, mean time to first token (TTFT), and decode throughput in tokens per second (TPS). Task latency includes both model inference and tool execution. Component analyses also measure prefix-cache hit rate, tool-end-to-first-token delay, and pause wait, which includes the tool call latency of an interrupted session.

4.2 Main Results

Table 1 compares five baselines across different levels of concurrency, models, and topologies. Taken together, these results make TAO the strongest overall choice: it combines consistently low latency and TTFT with high decode throughput more effectively than any single baseline, consistent with our focus on responsiveness after tool calls and improved KV reuse.

DeepSeek-V4 Flash.

We evaluate on challenging benchmarks with moderate concurrency. On SWE-Lite, , relative to the best competing method in each column, latency falls by 2.4–26.8%, TTFT by 7.4–36.3%, and decode throughput rises by 5.1–29.5%. On Terminal-Bench, TAO also leads on latency and TTFT at all three concurrency levels.

Qwen3-32B.

We use higher concurrency to exercise the serving capacity of its smaller model replicas. On SWE-Lite, TAO achieves the lowest TTFT at all three worker counts and the highest decode throughput at 96, 128 and 160 workers. On SWE-verified, TAO leads on TTFT and decode throughput throughout, with reductions of 12.9–29.9% in TTFT and gains of 4.0–7.8% in decode throughput. It also reduces latency by 8.3% and 9.0% at 96 and 160 workers; at 128 workers, latency is 2.5% higher than ThunderAgent.

GLM-4.7.

As a larger-model setting, GLM-4.7 provides a high-concurrency extensibility showcase on one node with 8×8\timesH100. Table 2 reports the separate worker-grouped results: on SWE-Lite at 160 workers, improvements reach 15.5% in latency, 14.05% in TTFT, and 20.48% in decode throughput. On all 500 SWE-verified tasks, TAO reduces mean task latency by 16.2–18.9% and client TTFT by 15.7–38.4%, while increasing decode throughput by 22.8–24.7% relative to ThunderAgent, the SOTA baseline on each metric.

Source of Improvement.

Figure 4 illustrates the serving dynamics at 160 workers. During the middle of the serving window, TAO processes ongoing requests more efficiently and steadily admits additional sessions under limited capacity, avoiding sharp bursts in concurrency. Appendix D provides the corresponding traces at other workers.

Compatibility.

TAO supports heterogeneous agent workloads and composes with engine-level KV-cache management. Table 3 evaluates a mixture of Terminal-Bench and SWE-Lite alongside AutomationBench at 32, 64, and 128 workers, reporting the available results. Appendix E.2 demonstrates integration with TokenCake (Bian et al., 2025) and discusses the relationship to program-aware scheduling in Agentix (Luo et al., 2026) and workflow-aware cache management. Appendix E.1 provides the complementary low-concurrency DeepSeek evaluation on a single TP8 replica.

4.3 Improvement Breakdown

As shown in Section 4.2, the worker sweep exposes a latency–throughput tradeoff: the lowest latency and TTFT occur at the smallest worker count, while peak decode throughput occurs at 64 workers for DeepSeek SWE-Lite and Terminal-Bench, 128 workers for Qwen SWE-Lite, and 96 workers for SWE-verified. We use DeepSeek at 32 workers as a balanced operating point and examine how cache-aware valuation, tool readiness, and joint placement improve reuse, tool-return responsiveness, and admission decisions.

Cache-aware valuation.

In a fixed-workload replay of 218 tasks with DP placement held fixed for the ThunderAgent control and cache-aware variants, cache-token ordering raises prefix-cache hit rate by 0.19 percentage points and reduces mean pause wait by 4.5% relative to ThunderAgent. Adding cache-credit decay raises hit rate by 0.31 percentage points and decode throughput by 1.68% relative to ThunderAgent. Figure 5 summarizes these changes; bars are percentage points for cache hit and percentages for the other metrics, with positive values denoting improvement.

Tool readiness.

Enabling readiness in the paired SWE-Lite runs increases decode throughput by 4.03% and reduces tool-end-to-first-token delay by 10.88%. Mean pause wait falls from 1.067 to 0.972 s. Figure 6 shows the return-delay distributions and prediction error. Across 10,967 completed tools, the final duration prediction has a mean absolute error of 0.410 s, with 82.9% of errors within 0.5 s.

The return-delay CDFs show that readiness shifts model responses earlier after tool completion. The middle panel summarizes the serving gains, and the right panel shows the prediction accuracy that informs readiness valuation. The return CDFs contain 10,481 and 10,673 observations, and the prediction panel contains 10,967 predictions.

Joint Scheduling.

Joint optimization improves the lexicographic scheduling objective in six of the 23 replay snapshots with multiple candidates (26.1%), matching the short-first heuristic in the remaining 17. Across all 35 reconstructable snapshots, including single-candidate cases, DP improves six (17.1%) and matches the heuristic in 29 (82.9%). Detailed cache-credit and admission examples appear in Appendix H.

4.4 Component Ablations

Table 4 compares the complete TAO configuration with variants of its value function, pause ordering, and resumption planner. The complete configuration achieves the highest decode throughput and cache-hit rate, together with the lowest mean TTFT, post-tool delay, and pause wait. Removing cache credit lowers decode throughput from 1417.97 to 1398.35 tok/s; removing readiness lowers it to 1363.06 tok/s. Using the pause ordering from ThunderAgent yields 1355.20 tok/s, while replacing DP resumption with best-fit-decreasing (BFD) yields 1233.72 tok/s. Both valuation and decision making contribute to the observed performance.

5 Related Work

PagedAttention and RadixAttention improve engine-level KV management, while Preble, Mooncake, and Dynamo exploit distributed cache locality (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2025). SMetric combines session affinity with load balancing (Wang et al., 2026a), and production schedulers support extensible scoring (Guy et al., 2025). Autellix prioritizes programs using service history, while ThunderAgent introduces the lifecycle and waiting pool on which TAO builds (Luo et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026). InferCept and Continuum manage KV retention across tool calls, with Continuum using historical tool-duration distributions (Abhyankar et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). TAO brings cache opportunity and tool readiness into a joint scheduler-level admission and placement objective, complementing engine-level KV management. Parrot and Helium exploit workflow dependencies, while KVFlow and CacheScout guide residency or prefetching using execution structure (Lin et al., 2024; Wadlom et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). TOPAS jointly considers prefix residency and admission through bounded search and greedy packing (Ni et al., 2026). Conveyor, Sutradhara, and PASTE reduce exposed tool latency through partial execution, overlap, or speculation (Xu et al., 2024; Biswas et al., 2026; Sui et al., 2026). TAO converts tool timing into near-term model-service opportunities that inform joint admission and placement. AgentSysBench and MARS motivate accounting for tool delays and deployment boundaries (Chang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). TAO couples an agentic value interface with joint placement and asynchronous revalidation, using the insights from classical multiple-knapsack and generalized-assignment machinery (Kellerer et al., 2004; Shmoys and Tardos, 1993). It becomes popular to formulate some optimization problems in LLM and agentic serving and solve online, from edge scenarios (Li et al., 2026) to large-scale infrastructure (Bu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026).

6 Conclusion

Tool execution makes agentic inference demand intermittent, while accumulated context makes the choice of node consequential. TAO brings these two properties into a common scheduling objective through cache credit, tool-return readiness, and token footprint. Joint dynamic-programming placement maximizes this objective under snapshot capacity constraints, and asynchronous revalidation connects the plan to live execution. Across the evaluated DeepSeek-V4 Flash and Qwen3-32B settings, this design delivers improvements of up to 26.8% in latency, 36.3% in mean TTFT, and 29.5% in decode throughput. The resulting architecture gives agentic serving an extensible way to translate workload knowledge into coordinated admission and placement.

AI use statement

We used generative AI tools to assist with manuscript editing and wording review. We did not use generative AI to run experiments, fabricate measurements, or decide which experimental artifacts are valid. We reviewed all AI-assisted text and figure suggestions against the source code, experiment records, cited literature, and the compiled manuscript. Appendix A Historical Tool-Duration Estimator

The history-based predictor in Section 3.4 uses a lightweight summary of completed calls. A finite-sample margin augments the historical mean, allowing the estimate to account for observed variability and the amount of available history.

For calls without direct timing evidence, we maintain statistics of completed durations keyed by the structured tool name ff. Let nfn_{f}, d¯f\bar{d}_{f}, sf2s_{f}^{2}, and RfR_{f} denote the sample count, mean, sample variance, and observed duration range. We use the following conservative upper estimate as a duration heuristic (Maurer and Pontil, 2009):

D^f={d¯f,nf=1,d¯f+2​sf2​log⁡(3/δ)nf+3​Rf​log⁡(3/δ)nf,nf≥2,\widehat{D}_{f}=\begin{cases}\bar{d}_{f},&n_{f}=1,\\[2.0pt] \displaystyle\bar{d}_{f}+\sqrt{\frac{2s_{f}^{2}\log(3/\delta)}{n_{f}}}+\frac{3R_{f}\log(3/\delta)}{n_{f}},&n_{f}\geq 2,\end{cases} (8)

with δ=0.2\delta=0.2. We use global completed-call statistics when tool-specific history is empty. Subtracting elapsed time from D^f\widehat{D}_{f} gives the remaining-duration estimate. The finite-sample margin is a scheduling heuristic; it does not provide calibrated coverage for an individual call. Continuum also exploits tool-duration history to choose a KV-retention TTL (Li et al., 2025). Our estimate converts this historical timing evidence into a signal for scheduler admission.

If both tool-specific and global histories are empty, the implementation uses a five-second duration default. The remaining-time estimate subtracts elapsed time and clips at zero, as in equation (5). Exposed timing hints take precedence as described in the main text.

Appendix B Extended Method Details

B.1 Joint selection and placement algorithm

At every scheduling time, wiw_{i} is updated with the memory demand of the total token count minus the shared token capacity for session ii, and CbC_{b} is updated with the remaining capacity of node bb from the metric observation. Algorithm B.1 summarizes TAO, from session evaluation to joint scheduling and live-state revalidation.

B.2 Asynchronous execution

The scheduler solves a frozen snapshot in an isolated worker. Before applying the plan, it checks that selected agent sessions remain eligible and match their recorded state signatures, then applies the longest prefix permitted by current capacities. Changed selected-agent session signatures cause the plan to be discarded. Revalidation preserves feasibility under current admission constraints. We quantify the effect of stale values, discarded plans, and partial application through a loss bound relative to the fresh-snapshot optimum, and measure these execution outcomes alongside solve time and plan age.

Conditional loss bound.

Let ss and tt be planning and application times, xsx_{s} the exact snapshot plan, and yty_{t} the revalidated plan (empty if discarded). Write 𝒳sΔ\mathcal{X}_{s}^{\Delta} and 𝒳tΔ\mathcal{X}_{t}^{\Delta} for the quantized feasible sets. For analysis, represent the lexicographic objective by one fixed scalar score UτU_{\tau} that preserves its order on the finite plans and values under comparison; the implementation still compares vectors. Define

ϵs,t\displaystyle\epsilon_{s,t} =maxx∈𝒳sΔ⁡|Ut​(x)−Us​(x)|,\displaystyle=\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{s}^{\Delta}}|U_{t}(x)-U_{s}(x)|,
As,t\displaystyle A_{s,t} =maxx∈𝒳tΔ⁡Ut​(x)−maxx∈𝒳sΔ∩𝒳tΔ⁡Ut​(x),\displaystyle=\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{t}^{\Delta}}U_{t}(x)-\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{s}^{\Delta}\cap\mathcal{X}_{t}^{\Delta}}U_{t}(x),
Ts,t\displaystyle T_{s,t} =[Ut​(xs)−Ut​(yt)]+.\displaystyle=[U_{t}(x_{s})-U_{t}(y_{t})]_{+}. (9)

These terms capture value drift, opportunities introduced by feasibility changes, and value lost during execution. The empty plan ensures a nonempty intersection. Then

maxx∈𝒳tΔ⁡Ut​(x)−Ut​(yt)≤As,t+2​ϵs,t+Ts,t.\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{t}^{\Delta}}U_{t}(x)-U_{t}(y_{t})\leq A_{s,t}+2\epsilon_{s,t}+T_{s,t}. (10)

The proof in Appendix C inserts the best common feasible plan and applies snapshot optimality plus two value-drift terms. If every plan has at most KK assignments and each scalar assignment value changes by at most ηs,t\eta_{s,t}, then ϵs,t≤K​ηs,t\epsilon_{s,t}\leq K\eta_{s,t}. With an additional drift bound ηs,t≤L⁡(t−s)\eta_{s,t}\leq L(t-s), the value-drift term becomes 2​K​L​(t−s)2KL(t-s); readiness jumps require separate allowances. An unquantized comparator adds the quantization gap, and a fallback adds its snapshot suboptimality gap.

The bound connects planner freshness to retained scheduling value: short plan age limits value drift under the stated assumptions, while revalidation losses appear explicitly in Ts,tT_{s,t}. Its comparator is the fresh placement optimum on the same realized state; Appendix C details this scope.

Appendix C Asynchronous Snapshot Loss: Proof and Scope

Loss relative to a fresh snapshot.

We compare the applied plan with the optimal placement at application time on the same observed system state. Let ss be the planning time and tt the application time. Write 𝒳sΔ\mathcal{X}_{s}^{\Delta} and 𝒳tΔ\mathcal{X}_{t}^{\Delta} for the discretized feasible sets, embedding both in the union of candidate–node assignments. The empty plan belongs to both sets. Let xsx_{s} be the exact snapshot solution and yt∈𝒳ty_{t}\in\mathcal{X}_{t} the applied plan, feasible under the current admission contract; a discarded plan has yt=0y_{t}=0.

To express loss numerically, let Uτ​(x)U_{\tau}(x) be a fixed positive weighted sum of the objective coordinates in equation (3), with weights that preserve their lexicographic order on the finite collection of plans and objective values considered at ss and tt. Such weights exist for finite sets, with a scale determined by the coordinate ranges and gaps. The scalar score serves the analysis; the implementation compares vectors directly. In particular, xsx_{s} maximizes UsU_{s} over 𝒳sΔ\mathcal{X}_{s}^{\Delta}. Extend the additive objective to all assignments in the union, including plans that have become infeasible.

Define the value variation, loss from changes in feasibility, and execution loss as

ϵs,t\displaystyle\epsilon_{s,t} =maxx∈𝒳sΔ⁡|Ut​(x)−Us​(x)|,\displaystyle=\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{s}^{\Delta}}|U_{t}(x)-U_{s}(x)|,
As,t\displaystyle A_{s,t} =maxx∈𝒳tΔ⁡Ut​(x)−maxx∈𝒳sΔ∩𝒳tΔ⁡Ut​(x),\displaystyle=\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{t}^{\Delta}}U_{t}(x)-\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{s}^{\Delta}\cap\mathcal{X}_{t}^{\Delta}}U_{t}(x),
Ts,t\displaystyle T_{s,t} =[Ut​(xs)−Ut​(yt)]+.\displaystyle=[U_{t}(x_{s})-U_{t}(y_{t})]_{+}. (11)

Here [z]+=max⁡(z,0)[z]_{+}=\max(z,0). New candidates, new eligibility, and additional capacity can contribute to As,tA_{s,t}; truncation or discard contributes to Ts,tT_{s,t}. Changes in feature values contribute to ϵs,t\epsilon_{s,t}.

Conditional bound.

For every exact snapshot solve and feasible applied plan,

maxx∈𝒳tΔ⁡Ut​(x)−Ut​(yt)≤As,t+2​ϵs,t+Ts,t.\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{t}^{\Delta}}U_{t}(x)-U_{t}(y_{t})\leq A_{s,t}+2\epsilon_{s,t}+T_{s,t}. (12)

To prove this, choose zz maximizing UtU_{t} over the intersection of the two feasible sets. Snapshot optimality gives Us​(z)≤Us​(xs)U_{s}(z)\leq U_{s}(x_{s}), and hence

Ut​(z)−Ut​(yt)\displaystyle U_{t}(z)-U_{t}(y_{t}) ≤[Ut​(z)−Us​(z)]+[Us​(xs)−Ut​(xs)]\displaystyle\leq[U_{t}(z)-U_{s}(z)]+[U_{s}(x_{s})-U_{t}(x_{s})]
+[Ut​(xs)−Ut​(yt)]≤2​ϵs,t+Ts,t.\displaystyle\quad+[U_{t}(x_{s})-U_{t}(y_{t})]\leq 2\epsilon_{s,t}+T_{s,t}.

Adding As,tA_{s,t} proves equation (12). If the comparator uses the original, undiscretized capacities, add the nonnegative quantization gap Qt=maxx∈𝒳t⁡Ut​(x)−maxx∈𝒳tΔ⁡Ut​(x)Q_{t}=\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{t}}U_{t}(x)-\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{t}^{\Delta}}U_{t}(x) to its right-hand side.

The bound isolates conditions under which asynchronous planning retains value. If every plan contains at most KK assignments and each scalar assignment value changes by at most ηs,t\eta_{s,t}, then ϵs,t≤K​ηs,t\epsilon_{s,t}\leq K\eta_{s,t}. A further assumption ηs,t≤L⁡(t−s)\eta_{s,t}\leq L(t-s) yields a variation term 2​K​L​(t−s)2KL(t-s); binary readiness require explicit jump allowances and do not satisfy this assumption automatically. Summing equation (12) over scheduling ticks bounds cumulative loss against fresh-snapshot optima on the realized states, using one common scalarization. It does not bound end-to-end latency or regret against a globally optimal online policy, whose earlier decisions can produce different future states. A uniform numerical bound requires corresponding bounds on state variation, feasibility changes, and discarded value. A fallback solve additionally contributes its snapshot suboptimality gap.

Figures 7 and 8 extend Figure 4 to 96 and 128 workers on the 300-task SWE-Lite workload with GLM-4.7 TP8. Appendix E Compatibility

E.1 Fallback Compatibility

Table 5 evaluates five schedulers on a single TP8 node across 4–64 workers. Each run serves the 300-task SWE-Lite workload through MiniSWE. This experiment checks that TAO remains competitive when concurrency is low and scheduling has less opportunity to improve performance. At 4–8 workers, its mean task latency stays within 2.3% of the best baseline, it retains over 92% of the best baseline’s decode throughput, and its mean TTFT is only 15–20 ms above the best baseline. Thus, TAO incurs little task-latency degradation at low concurrency while maintaining competitive throughput. Together with its leading performance in the main evaluation (Section 4.2), this fallback behavior supports choosing TAO as the default scheduler across the evaluated operating regimes.

E.2 KV-Cache Management Compatibility

TokenCake uses workflow dependencies and agent priorities to guide its Space Scheduler, and tool-stall events and timing prediction to guide offload and upload in its Time Scheduler (Bian et al., 2025). Agentix prioritizes and preempts LLM calls using program-level service history to reduce request- and program-level blocking (Luo et al., 2026). It operates at the request-scheduling layer, so integrating it with TAO would require coordinating the two admission policies. KVFlow represents a workflow as an Agent Step Graph and uses steps-to-execution to prioritize cache eviction and prefetching (Pan et al., 2025). CacheScout learns execution transitions online to guide cache management without requiring a predefined graph (Zhang et al., 2026). These mechanisms provide information about future cache use. In our formulation, such information can inform the program–node values supplied to session evaluation, while engine-local cache policies can operate beneath TAO’s admission and placement decisions. This is an architectural extension for KVFlow and CacheScout, while the implemented composition evaluated here uses TokenCake.

With TokenCake enabled, the combined system completes validated 300-task SWE-Lite runs on DeepSeek-V4 Flash TP4×\times2 at 16 and 32 workers. Relative to the same engine behind consistent-hash routing, the combination increases decode throughput from 785.159 to 886.772 tok/s and from 1292.584 to 1347.373 tok/s, respectively (12.9% and 4.2%). These runs establish operational compatibility.

Table 6 compares three frontends over the TokenCake engine. At 16 and 32 workers, TAO lowers mean task latency relative to consistent hashing by 3.1% and 2.0%, while increasing decode throughput by 12.9% and 4.2%. At 32 workers, client TTFT increases slightly from 0.220 to 0.223 s. Both combined runs record balanced request routing across the two replicas (5816/5393 and 5328/5683 requests) and tool-prediction updates (22085 and 21776). Neither records a program pause, resume, or migration, and their final offload series are absent. The evidence therefore establishes lifecycle and serving compatibility under these loads; attribution to DP selection or overlapping offload would require runs that activate those mechanisms. Separate transfer qualifications verify actual GPU–CPU movement.

Appendix F InferenceX Replay

TAO also achieves the highest decode throughput at every tested concurrency level on InferenceX, a fixed trace corpus served by DeepSeek on 2 nodes with 4×4\timesH100 per node. The replay uses 393 AgentX traces with a 1M-token context limit and 1,800-second profiling windows (SemiAnalysis, 2026a; SemiAnalysis, 2026b); workers count the concurrent session trees. Table 7 reports client-visible TTFT and decode throughput, together with seconds per request computed as 60/R60/R, where RR is native request throughput in requests per minute. This last metric is the reciprocal of aggregate request throughput within the profiling window.

Decode throughput improves on the best competing method by 4.2%, 1.8%, and 10.1% at 16, 32, and 64 workers, respectively. TAO also achieves the lowest TTFT at 16 workers; cache-aware scheduling has lower TTFT at 32 and 64 workers. Figure 9 shows the accompanying reuse advantage: TAO maintains the highest prefix-cache hit rate throughout, even as hit rates decrease with concurrency for all four methods.

Appendix G Sensitivity to longer tool-return delays

We examine how longer tool-return delays affect scheduling using a replay of SWE-Lite sessions recorded with MiniSWE. The replay fixes the source prompts, 6,995 model-request records, and 6,942 tool records, while model outputs are generated live. Each session receives a fixed additional tool-return delay drawn from 1–5 s; multipliers of 1, 2, and 4 produce additional delays of 1–5, 2–10, and 4–20 s, respectively. DeepSeek-V4 Flash runs on TP4×\times2 with 32 workers, a 33,024-token context limit, and a 512-token per-session reserve.

Table 8 compares three configurations: the historical TAO w/o readiness reference, TAO with structured-history tool-duration predictions, and Oracle with the replay’s known effective tool duration. The historical reference also disables cached-token decay and shared-token refresh, which both current configurations enable; comparisons with that reference therefore measure the combined configuration change. Acting-token decay remains disabled in both current configurations. All six current cells pass the replay validator, covering all 6,942 tool records. Each cell is a single exploratory run with batch-invariant execution disabled and live model generation.

TAO sustains gains as tool delays grow.

Relative to the historical configuration, TAO reduces makespan by 20.72%, 16.42%, and 19.28% and mean session latency by 21.57%, 20.57%, and 17.91% at scales 1, 2, and 4, respectively. These gains span additional tool-return delays from 1–5 s to 4–20 s.

Longer delays make readiness relevant to more placement decisions.

For TAO, removing readiness from the same captured state changes 11/668 (1.65%), 53/1,345 (3.94%), and 200/2,521 (7.93%) of the exact DP plan comparisons at multipliers 1, 2, and 4. The rate increases by 6.29 percentage points from scale 1 to scale 4, indicating that tool-return timing affects a growing fraction of placement decisions as delays lengthen. These same-state comparisons isolate readiness’s effect on individual placement decisions within the TAO runs.

History-based predictions approach oracle runtime performance.

Providing the known replay duration reduces mean absolute prediction error by 99.53–99.69%, to 0.025–0.030 s. At scale 2, it also reduces makespan by 2.24% and mean session latency by 0.71% relative to TAO. Across all three scales, the signed makespan improvements range from −0.10-0.10% to +2.24%, and mean session-latency improvements range from −0.36-0.36% to +0.71%. Thus, the history-based predictor achieves runtime performance close to the accurate-timing variant in this sweep, even as longer delays increase the frequency of readiness-sensitive decisions.

Reconstructed snapshots from the 32-worker DeepSeek replay show how joint placement preserves more cache value and admits more sessions than a short-first heuristic (Section 4.3). The figures compare scheduler-level assignment decisions and their cache credit; vLLM manages the physical KV cache. The short-first heuristic is evaluated offline on the same snapshots.

Appendix I Scheduler Overhead Analysis

Across the four-replica Qwen runs at 96–160 workers, planning submissions rise from 98 to 1,681. At 160 workers, completed assignment solving averages 1.59 ms with a P95 of 3.68 ms; the two measured parts together account for 4.03 s (0.112% of the run). Thus, the recorded scheduling work remains below 0.12% at four replicas and up to 160 workers.

Table 9 expands the scheduling work and planner outcomes summarized above. State preparation runs synchronously in the scheduler, while the planner worker solves assignments asynchronously. Result delay measures dispatch, solving, and delivery together. The two- and four-replica deployments exercise this design under different models and concurrency levels.

The state budget bounds DP search, with best-fit-decreasing placement handling exhausted searches. Fallback occurs in 5.24% of submissions at 64 DeepSeek workers and 3.06–8.98% in the Qwen sweep. Measured work covers state preparation and completed solves; exhausted searches and fallback execution are untimed, so work/run is a partial accounting rather than a measure of CPU utilization or request-latency overhead. Discards and partial applications record how live revalidation handles state changes before application. The 16-worker DeepSeek run submits one plan, so its timing entry describes that single solve.

Appendix J Extended Related Work

Capacity-constrained optimization.

Dynamic programming and exact multiple-knapsack algorithms provide established tools for selecting items and assigning them to capacity-limited resources (Bellman, 1957; Kellerer et al., 2004; Pisinger, 1999). Node-dependent assignment values place our formulation within the multiple-knapsack/generalized-assignment family. Approximation algorithms address the computational cost of this family (Chekuri and Khanna, 2005; Shmoys and Tardos, 1993), while online resource-allocation algorithms analyze decisions under specified arrival models (Li et al., 2020). TAO uses this classical optimization machinery to connect agentic session evaluation with joint admission and node placement. Its additive, lexicographic objective makes cache opportunity, tool readiness, and token footprint precedence explicit, and its asynchronous executor revalidates assignments against live state. Section 3.5 and Appendix B.2 specify snapshot optimality and the bounds for asynchronous application.

KV locality and agent scheduling.

PagedAttention improves physical KV allocation and sharing, while SGLang’s RadixAttention reuses prefixes within the serving runtime (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024). Preble co-optimizes distributed prefix reuse and computation balance; Mooncake combines a distributed KV store with disaggregated serving (Srivatsa et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025). Dynamo and production gateways expose cache- and load-aware request scheduling (NVIDIA, 2025; vLLM Production Stack Team, n.d.; SGLang Team, n.d.), and llm-d provides pluggable scoring components (Guy et al., 2025). SMetric exploits session structure by balancing first-turn requests and assigning later turns to nodes with reusable cache, using a global cache tier to limit the cost of redistribution (Wang et al., 2026a). TAO builds on these locality and load-balancing principles with joint optimization of assignments for waiting agent sessions under shared capacity. This joint view accounts for how one admission consumes capacity needed by other session–node assignments.

Program-level schedulers also preserve information across model calls. Autellix uses attained service and critical-path information to prioritize single-threaded and distributed programs (Luo et al., 2025). ThunderAgent introduces the program abstraction, state-aware pausing, elapsed-time discounting of tool execution programs’ effective token demand, and a global waiting queue (Kang et al., 2026). TAO adds node-specific cache values and readiness to the joint placement objective. Tool-gap cache management addresses a complementary decision: InferCept chooses among preservation, swapping, and recomputation by modeling resource waste (Abhyankar et al., 2024); Continuum selects a cache-retention TTL using historical tool-duration distributions, reconstruction cost, and returning programs’ queueing cost, together with TTL-aware program ordering (Li et al., 2025). These systems control physical KV retention. TAO coordinates scheduler-level admission opportunities, with predicted readiness distinguishing plans that have equal higher-precedence cache value. The serving engine controls the resulting cache residency.

Workflow, prediction, and tool execution.

Workflow structure provides information beyond an isolated request. Parrot exposes inter-request dependencies through Semantic Variables, and Helium compiles workflow query plans for proactive reuse and cache-aware execution (Lin et al., 2024; Wadlom et al., 2026). KVFlow uses an Agent Step Graph and steps-to-execution to guide eviction and prefetching (Pan et al., 2025); CacheScout learns execution transitions online without a predefined graph (Zhang et al., 2026). Their predictions guide context residency and prefetching; readiness supplies a binary near-term admission-opportunity signal derived from tool timing. SAGA combines workflow graphs, session-affinity batching, and work stealing (Guo et al., 2026). TOPAS also uses heuristic state searching: it scores prefix-residency and request-admission states using remaining workflow paths, movement costs, and downstream reuse, with bounded candidate search and greedy packing (Ni et al., 2026). Its task-dependent utility and engine-level residency decisions differ from our fixed additive value contract and exact multi-node scheduling problem.

Prediction also supports latency-oriented scheduling. ELIS predicts response length, while Kairos combines workflow-aware priority with memory-aware dispatch (Choi et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Recent work separates already-ready turns from their release, using a mean–CVaR objective and an adaptive budget for committed inference work (Feng et al., 2026). This addresses tail-aware release after dependencies complete; TAO additionally evaluates near-term return opportunities during external tool execution. Complementary mechanisms change the execution timeline itself: Conveyor exposes partial tool execution, Sutradhara overlaps tool work and prefill through orchestrator–engine cooperation, and PASTE speculates on future tools while coordinating tool execution with returning model agent sessions (Xu et al., 2024; Biswas et al., 2026; Sui et al., 2026). SmoothAgent prepares transformed context on a lookahead stream, and Pie exposes programmable generation and KV handlers (Pan et al., 2026; Gim et al., 2025). TAO operates in the scheduler, using timing evidence to coordinate admission and node placement.

Deployment and workloads.

AgentSysBench documents substantial non-LLM latency and deployment-dependent resource demands (Chang et al., 2026). MARS explicitly coordinates GPU inference, CPU tool pressure, admission, and KV retention in heterogeneous serving (Wang et al., 2026b). In our CGDC scenario, distributed executors manage tool CPU and memory, and their resource pressure reaches the GPU scheduler through tool-return timing. TAO captures this interaction through readiness when allocating GPU admission capacity. OpenHands supports separate execution environments (Wang et al., 2025). Coding and terminal workloads, together with InferenceX/AgentX trace replay, provide complementary evidence about task completion and serving behavior (mini-SWE-agent Contributors, 2026; Jimenez et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026; SemiAnalysis, 2026b; SemiAnalysis, 2026a), with workload-specific timing metrics defined in the evaluation.
